title: Compositional Visual Planning via Inference-Time Diffusion Scaling
one_liner: Long-horizon robot plans are stable when boundary agreement is enforced on clean data estimates, not noisy intermediate steps, using message passing across overlapping chunks.
lead: A robot needs to plan a long sequence of moves (e.g., move arm, grasp, lift, place). Diffusion models are good at short sequences, but stitching short plans together breaks down in noisy intermediate states. This paper enforces boundary agreement by working on cleaned predictions (Tweedie estimates) and using message passing to keep all chunks consistent as they overlap.

problem.h2: Long-horizon planning breaks when stitching short segments
paras: A robot arm needs to execute long tasks: pick an object off a shelf, carry it across a room, place it in a bin. Diffusion models (neural networks trained to predict cleaner versions of corrupted data) excel at short 10-frame plans. But a full task might need 100 frames, far beyond training.

Existing methods try to solve this by breaking the long task into overlapping short chunks, run each through the short-horizon model separately, then stitch the overlaps together by averaging. The problem: diffusion models work through intermediate noisy steps. When you stitch overlaps in noisy space, the boundary where chunks meet has no real consistency — one chunk says the arm is here, its neighbor says it is there. The noisy data space is unstable, and small disagreements at boundaries cascade into broken plans.

callout.html: The paper enforces boundary agreement on clean data estimates instead of noisy intermediate steps, keeping long-horizon plans globally consistent.

panels.title: 1. Short clips work
panels.caption: Diffusion models trained on 10-frame clips output stable plans.

panels.title: 4. Message passing enforces agreement

panels.title: 5. Stable long-horizon plan

steps.text: Split long 100-frame task into 10-frame overlapping segments.
Pass each through the short-horizon diffusion model in denoising loop.
At each step, read Tweedie estimate: what is the true image according to the model right now?
Use message passing to make overlap regions agree across chunks.
Steer diffusion updates toward the agreement without losing diversity.

paras: Instead of averaging noisy intermediate states, the method operates on Tweedie estimates: the clean data prediction the model makes at each step. This shift from noisy to clean unlocks global consistency because the clean space is stable enough to enforce hard boundary constraints.

hidden.name: Boundary consistency score
paras: At each frame where two chunks overlap, there is a mismatch: Chunk-A predicts the arm is at position X, Chunk-B predicts Y. Boundary consistency measures this gap. In noisy space, small differences grow unstably. The paper does not measure this directly as a number, but enforces it implicitly: message passing iteratively reduces boundary disagreement until all chunks agree on the same clean transition.

The method estimates this by computing a residual: how far is the current Tweedie estimate from agreeing across the boundary? That residual feeds back into the diffusion guidance, steering the model toward agreement.

heat.caption: Darker means closer to clean boundary agreement. Highlights show where message passing operates.

reads.html: Boundary consistency is the degree to which overlapping regions of adjacent chunks predict the same arm position and motion.
The loss Lsync enforces hard consistency across boundaries by penalizing residuals in Tweedie-estimate space, while asynchronous message passing relaxes this for stable convergence.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the real mechanism
paras: The core insight: diffusion models output a noisy-to-clean sequence, and the intermediate noisy space is chaotic. Boundaries enforced in noise jitter and drift. But at each step, the model also predicts what the true clean data is (the Tweedie estimate). That clean space is stable enough to enforce hard constraints.

Here is why message passing works: when Chunk-A and Chunk-B overlap, their Tweedie estimates can disagree. A loss term (Lsync) computes this disagreement as a penalty. Synchronous message passing applies this penalty to all chunks at once, which is fast but can be jerky. Asynchronous message passing updates chunks one at a time, which converges slower but more smoothly. The paper uses both: synchronous for speed and asynchronous to stabilize. Then diffusion-sphere guidance takes the residual penalty and converts it to a steering term in the diffusion update, nudging the model toward agreement at each denoising step without collapsing diversity.

stages.s: Apply sync and async message passing

math.words: The synchronous loss penalizes how far estimated clean boundaries are from each other. A smaller value means better agreement.
math.equation: Lsync = sum over boundaries of (boundary_residual_squared) = sum_i (chunk_i_clean - chunk_i+1_clean)^2
symbols: Tweedie estimate at boundary of chunk i
Tweedie estimate at boundary of chunk i+1

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Imagine two overlapping chunks with clean boundary estimates.
Chunk-A predicts arm position = 50.0, Chunk-B predicts 48.0.
After message passing, both update: Chunk-A -> 49.0, Chunk-B -> 49.0.
The loss falls, and guidance steers future steps toward 49.0.

math.note: The method does not solve this loss in advance; instead, it uses the residual as a per-step nudge during diffusion, making updates gradually agreeable without retraining.

bars.h2: Quality comparison: naive stitching vs. this paper

charts.title: Naive stitching in noisy space
charts.note: Boundaries in noisy space drift and accumulate error, failing on new combinations.

charts.title: This paper: clean-space boundaries + message passing
charts.note: Enforcing agreement in clean space stabilizes the method across new tasks and start-goal pairs.

items.html: Locking all chunks at once fights local dynamics. Solution: the paper adds asynchronous updates (one chunk at a time) to speed convergence while keeping stability.

items.b: Guidance can collapse diversity in the plan.
items.html: If the boundary penalty is too strong, all samples converge to one boring trajectory. Solution: diffusion-sphere guidance interpolates between base diffusion and penalty, preserving randomness.

items.b: Long sequences still have memory cost.
items.html: Message passing across 100-frame sequences requires storing intermediate states. Practical limits depend on hardware. The paper tests up to 100 frames; longer sequences would need approximations.

items.b: Done right: boundary consistency works at test time.
items.html: No retraining needed; the method is training-free. A frozen short-horizon model works for any new start-goal pair, including ones never seen during training.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy robot planner: train a short-horizon diffusion model on 10-frame pick-and-place clips. Then at test time, compose a 50-frame unseen task (e.g., start at new position, place in new location). Compare naive stitching in noise vs. the paper's message-passing method. Measure success: does the generated plan, when fed to an inverse model, achieve the goal without colliding?
demo.closing: The demo proves the key claim: enforcing boundary agreement in clean space (Tweedie estimates) via message passing generalizes to unseen start-goal combinations that naive stitching fails on.
